title: MesoNet achieves 56.2% test accuracy at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic via IMP with global thresholds
content: MesoNet, pruned using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with global thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, applied uniformly across convolutional and MLP layers, Adam optimizer with learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10), achieves 56.2% test accuracy at 80% sparsity on the OpenForensic dataset, using approximately 3,000 parameters (0.003M). This accuracy corresponds to 89.8% of the dense model's baseline accuracy (62.6%), demonstrating that a highly compressed MesoNet subnetwork preserves most of the original detection performance on this dataset.

title: CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet maintain near-baseline accuracy at 80% sparsity on OpenForensic via IMP with global thresholds
content: For CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic dataset, Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) with global thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, uniformly across layers, Adam lr=$1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10) yields 80%-sparsity test accuracies of 90.88% (99.4% of the dense baseline 91.41%), 94.29% (99.9% of the dense baseline 94.3%), and 96.11% (99.9% of the dense baseline 96.20%), respectively. Thus, at 80% sparsity on this dataset, these architectures contain sparse subnetworks that preserve almost all original performance.

title: ResNet-18 achieves 83% accuracy at 80% sparsity on FaceForensics++ with IMP-local, outperforming dense baseline and IMP-global
content: For the FaceForensics++ dataset (a dataset of 11,600 training images from face-cropped frames of 400 videos with varied compression and deepfake generation artifacts), ResNet-18 pruned with Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) using local (per-layer) thresholds (20% weight removal per iteration for 8 rounds, Adam lr=$1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10) retains 83% test accuracy at 80% sparsity, outperforming both its dense baseline and the same network pruned using global thresholds. Thus, local pruning yields superior preservation of critical layer-specific features on compressed, challenging datasets.

title: Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) procedure and operational configuration for deepfake detection
content:
Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) for deepfake detection is implemented as follows: initialize binary mask $\mathbf{m}^{(0)} = \mathbf{1}$; for each pruning round $j=1,\dots,J$ (with $J=8$ rounds) train the network $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{m}^{(j-1)} \odot \theta^{(j-1)})$ for one cycle, compute a pruning threshold $\alpha^{(j)}$, and update the mask per-global or per-layer rules:
      $$
      \mathbf{m}_l^{(j)}[i] =
      \begin{cases}
      0 & \text{if } |\theta_l^{(j-1)}[i]| \leq \alpha^{(j)} \text{ (global) or } \alpha_l^{(j)} \text{ (local)},\\
      1 & \text{otherwise},
      \end{cases}
      $$
      then set $\theta^{(j)} = \mathbf{m}^{(j)} \odot \theta^{(j-1)}$. Experimentally, the pruning schedule removes 20% of weights per iteration (cumulative up to 80%), applied uniformly to convolutional and MLP layers; training uses Adam with learning rate $1\times 10^{-4}$, early stopping patience 10, and experiments are performed on a NVIDIA V4090 GPU. One-shot pruning corresponds to applying $\mathbf{m}^{(1)}$ after one full training cycle.

title: IMP, especially local IMP, consistently outperforms one-shot pruning at high sparsity across architectures and datasets
content: Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP), and in particular IMP with local (per-layer) thresholds, consistently outperforms one-shot magnitude pruning (pruning all weights in a single step after one full training cycle) across MesoNet, CNN-5, ResNet-18, and XceptionNet on the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets. The performance gap increases at sparsity levels above 70%: at 80% sparsity, IMP-Local yields a 1–2 percentage-point accuracy advantage over one-shot pruning on OpenForensic and up to a 2–3 percentage-point advantage on FaceForensics++ across these models. This indicates that iterative refinement better preserves subtle discriminative features needed for deepfake detection.

title: Pruning strategy effectiveness is dataset-dependent: global better on OpenForensic, local better on FaceForensics++
content: The effectiveness of global versus local pruning criteria in Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) is dataset-dependent. Global pruning (using a single threshold based on all weights) generalizes better and is more stable on the cleaner, less compressed OpenForensic dataset (140,000 training images, no face cropping). Local pruning (using per-layer thresholds) better preserves accuracy on the challenging, heavily compressed FaceForensics++ dataset (11,600 training images from 400 face-cropped videos with varied compression artifacts). This indicates that dataset statistics and compression artifacts determine which pruning strategy best preserves manipulation-sensitive features.

title: Grad-CAM shows pruned ResNet-18 models preserve attention on facial regions and shift toward high-frequency/temporal artifacts as sparsity increases
content: Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) comparisons between dense (0% sparsity) and pruned (60% and 80% sparsity) ResNet-18 models reveal that pruned subnetworks maintain concentrated attention on semantically meaningful facial regions, notably the cheek and eye areas, even at 80% sparsity, while the attention maps contract and focus on smaller regions. The attention difference is quantified via the Frobenius norm $\Delta L^c(p)=\| L_{\text{original}}^c - L_p^c \|_F$, where $L_{\text{original}}^c$ is the Grad-CAM heatmap for class $c$ from the original dense model and $L_p^c$ is the heatmap from the model at pruning rate $p$. Additionally, qualitative analysis of Grad-CAM heatmaps indicates that pruned networks increasingly emphasize high-frequency artifacts and temporal inconsistencies over broader semantic features as sparsity increases.

title: Sparse subnetworks discovered via IMP on OpenForensic transfer to FaceForensics++ with minor accuracy degradation or modest improvement
content: Sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) discovered via Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) on the larger OpenForensic dataset transfer effectively to the smaller FaceForensics++ dataset when evaluated directly (zero-shot) with no fine-tuning. At 60% sparsity, an IMP-pruned MesoNet achieves 61.2% accuracy on FaceForensics++, compared to its dense baseline accuracy on FaceForensics++ of 59.9%. At 80% sparsity, an IMP-pruned CNN-5 subnetwork achieves 74.5% accuracy (dense baseline on FaceForensics++: 76.2%) and an IMP-pruned ResNet-18 subnetwork achieves 83.7% accuracy (dense baseline: 85.3%). Thus, subnetworks found on a larger source dataset can be reused on a smaller target dataset with minor accuracy degradation or, in some cases, modest improvement.

title: ResNet-18 exhibits greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior than MesoNet under iterative magnitude pruning
content: Larger, deeper architectures such as ResNet-18 (11.7M parameters) exhibit greater redundancy and stronger lottery-ticket behavior (retaining near-original performance at high sparsity) on both the OpenForensic and FaceForensics++ datasets when pruned using Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP). Compact networks such as MesoNet (0.015M parameters) are more sensitive to pruning and degrade more quickly. This establishes an architecture-dependent trade-off between base model compactness and compressibility: starting with a larger model yields subnetworks that are both small and robust, while very compact models may lack sufficient redundancy to tolerate extreme pruning.

title: IMP yields better transferability than one-shot pruning across architectures and sparsity levels in zero-shot cross-dataset evaluation
content: In cross-dataset transfer experiments (zero-shot from OpenForensic to FaceForensics++), subnetworks produced by Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) consistently outperform one-shot-pruned subnetworks at both 60% and 80% sparsity across MesoNet, CNN-5, and ResNet-18. This indicates that iterative pruning produces subnetworks with superior generalization across datasets.
